best.none: No spots inside the loaded terrain.

layers.heading: Map layer
layers.sunLegend: Share of time the Sun is up, averaged over 19 years at 2.4 km. Dark blue 0% to yellow 92%.
layers.earthLegend: Share of time Earth is above the horizon, averaged over 19 years at 2.4 km. Dark blue 0% to yellow 100%.
layers.shadowLegend: Blue ground never sees the Sun over 19 years, where ice can survive.

checks.heading: How we checked it
checks.spice: Sun and Earth directions match NASA's SPICE toolkit at {{cases}} site-and-date cases: worst difference {{worst}} arcseconds, limit {{tol}}.
checks.sunlight: Long-term sunlight on {{terrain}} against published values (limit {{tol}} points):
checks.ridgeNote: △ Point A sits on a ridge narrower than one terrain pixel; finer terrain should close that gap.
checks.recorded: Recorded by the test suite on {{date}}.

report.heading: Site report
report.sun: Sun up for the whole stay
report.terrainCoarse: Terrain: NASA LOLA at {{km}} km per pixel. Narrow ridges and small hills are smoothed out, so treat this as a first pass.
report.flatWarning: Terrain is not loaded, so the horizon is treated as flat. Hills can hide the Sun and Earth earlier than shown here.
report.offTerrain: This spot is outside the loaded terrain, so the horizon is treated as flat.

reason.SUN_BELOW_HORIZON: The Sun drops below the horizon on <d>{{at}}</d>.
reason.EARTH_BELOW_HORIZON: Earth drops below the horizon on <d>{{at}}</d>.
reason.SLOPE_TOO_STEEP: The ground is too steep: <d>{{slope}}°</d> over 100 m.
reason.OUTSIDE_ZONE: This spot is more than 6° from the pole, outside NASA's Artemis zone.
reason.NO_DATA_ephemeris: No Sun and Earth data for these dates. SiteLine covers 2026 to 2035.
reason.NO_DATA_slope: The 100 m landing-slope rule needs terrain finer than what is loaded.

globe.hint: The Moon lit by the Sun for the landing date. Drag to turn it, scroll to zoom. Click near the south pole to check a spot there.

panel.heading: Earth
panel.empty: Click anywhere on the globe, or search for a country, to see what is there.
panel.sources: Borders, names and cities: <ne>Natural Earth</ne> (public domain). Imagery: <bmng>Blue Marble: Next Generation</bmng>, NASA Earth Observatory (Reto Stöckli), resampled; the map style recolours its land and fills the sea. Night lights: <bm>Black Marble 2016</bm>, NASA Earth Observatory images by Joshua Stevens, using Suomi NPP VIIRS data from Miguel Román, NASA GSFC, resampled. Details in CREDITS.md.

mars.hint: Drag to turn Mars, scroll to zoom, click a place to read its height and name. Heights are stretched, so mountains look taller than they are.
mars.searchPlaceholder: Find a crater, volcano or valley
mars.realSunHint: Lit by the real Sun for the landing date, as Mars turns.

kinds.AlbedoFeature: Geographic area distinguished by amount of reflected light
kinds.Cavus: Hollows, irregular steep-sided depressions usually in arrays or clusters
kinds.Labyrinthus: Complex of intersecting valleys or ridges.
kinds.Lingula: Extension of plateau having rounded lobate or tongue-like boundaries
kinds.Mensa: A flat-topped prominence with cliff-like edges
kinds.Patera: An irregular crater, or a complex one with scalloped edges
kinds.Serpens: Sinuous feature with segments of positive and negative relief along its length

panel.heading: Mars
panel.empty: Click anywhere on the planet, or search for a feature, to see what is there.
panel.sources: Heights: NASA MGS MOLA (<megdr>MEGDR</megdr>, made by the MOLA Science Team and archived by the PDS Geosciences Node at Washington University in St. Louis) through <jaanga>Jaanga’s height-map tiles</jaanga>, © 2015 Jaanga authors, <ccby>CC BY 4.0</ccby>, resampled to a coarser grid (about 21 km), so peaks and floors can read a few hundred metres off. Slope shading is computed from these heights, so it has no finer detail than they do. Colour: <sss>Solar System Scope</sss> Mars map, <ccby>CC BY 4.0</ccby>, based on NASA elevation and imagery data and recompressed; the site notes that unmapped gaps in its maps are filled with fictional terrain. Names and feature types: <gaz>IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature</gaz> (USGS), public domain. Details in CREDITS.md.
